claim: In many species, within-group conflict leads to immediate avoidance of potential aggressors or increases in affiliation.
source: In many species, within-group conflict leads to immediate avoidance of potential aggressors or increases in affiliation, but no studies have investigated delayed post-conflict management behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature on post-conflict behavior in the introduction section.

claim: No studies have investigated delayed post-conflict management behaviour.
source: In many species, within-group conflict leads to immediate avoidance of potential aggressors or increases in affiliation, but no studies have investigated delayed post-conflict management behaviour.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of the study.

claim: Bystanders take notice of vocalisations produced during foraging displacements in dwarf mongooses.
source: First, we used natural and playback-simulated foraging displacements to demonstrate that bystanders take notice of the vocalisations produced during such within-group conflict events but that they do not engage in any immediate post-conflict affiliative behaviour with the protagonists or other bystanders.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both natural observations and playback experiments showing increased vigilance.

claim: Bystanders do not engage in any immediate post-conflict affiliative behaviour with the protagonists or other bystanders following foraging displacements.
source: First, we used natural and playback-simulated foraging displacements to demonstrate that bystanders take notice of the vocalisations produced during such within-group conflict events but that they do not engage in any immediate post-conflict affiliative behaviour with the protagonists or other bystanders.
evidence: This claim is supported by observational and experimental data showing no grooming occurred in the immediate aftermath.

claim: Fewer individuals groomed on evenings following an afternoon of simulated conflict compared to control evenings.
source: Overall, fewer individuals groomed on evenings following an afternoon of simulated conflict, but those that did groomed more than on control evenings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 showing reduced proportion of individuals grooming.

claim: Individuals that groomed on conflict evenings groomed more than on control evenings.
source: Overall, fewer individuals groomed on evenings following an afternoon of simulated conflict, but those that did groomed more than on control evenings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased proportion of time spent grooming by those who participated.

claim: Subordinate bystanders groomed with the simulated aggressor significantly less on conflict compared to control evenings.
source: Subordinate bystanders groomed with the simulated aggressor significantly less, and groomed more with one another, on conflict compared to control evenings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 showing reduced grooming with simulated aggressors.

claim: Subordinate bystanders groomed more with one another on conflict compared to control evenings.
source: Subordinate bystanders groomed with the simulated aggressor significantly less, and groomed more with one another, on conflict compared to control evenings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased subordinate-subordinate grooming bout duration.

claim: Dwarf mongooses acoustically obtain information about within-group contests including protagonist identity.
source: Our study provides experimental evidence that dwarf mongooses acoustically obtain information about within-group contests (including protagonist identity), retain that information, and use it to inform conflict-management decisions with a temporal delay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential responses to simulated aggressors versus non-playback dominants.

claim: Dwarf mongooses retain information about within-group contests.
source: Our study provides experimental evidence that dwarf mongooses acoustically obtain information about within-group contests (including protagonist identity), retain that information, and use it to inform conflict-management decisions with a temporal delay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing delayed behavioral responses 30-60 minutes after playbacks.

claim: Dwarf mongooses use information about within-group contests to inform conflict-management decisions with a temporal delay.
source: Our study provides experimental evidence that dwarf mongooses acoustically obtain information about within-group contests (including protagonist identity), retain that information, and use it to inform conflict-management decisions with a temporal delay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in grooming patterns at the evening refuge following afternoon playbacks.

claim: Within-group conflict can be costly in terms of injury and mortality, time and energy expenditure, increased stress, and disrupted social relationships.
source: Within-group conflict, especially if it escalates to aggression, can be costly in terms of injury and mortality, time and energy expenditure, increased stress, and disrupted social relationships (Aureli, 1997; Aureli et al., 2002; de Waal, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Conflict-management strategies that minimise costs have evolved in many species.
source: Conflict-management strategies that minimise these costs, either by reducing the likelihood of aggressive escalation in the first place or by mitigating the consequences of such physical contests when they do arise, have therefore evolved in many species (Aureli et al., 2002; Aureli and de Waal, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many studies have documented increases in affiliation between former opponents in the aftermath of a contest (reconciliation).
source: Much of the early work on post-conflict behaviour focussed on interactions between the protagonists (the aggressor and the target): many studies have documented increases in affiliation between former opponents in the aftermath of a contest (reconciliation; Aureli et al., 2002; de Waal, 2000; de Waal and van Roosmalen, 1979), although there are also examples of victims avoiding aggressors (wariness; Benkada et al., 2020; Kutsukake and Clutton-Brock, 2008; Sommer et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on reconciliation.

claim: There are examples of victims avoiding aggressors (wariness) after contests.
source: Much of the early work on post-conflict behaviour focussed on interactions between the protagonists (the aggressor and the target): many studies have documented increases in affiliation between former opponents in the aftermath of a contest (reconciliation; Aureli et al., 2002; de Waal, 2000; de Waal and van Roosmalen, 1979), although there are also examples of victims avoiding aggressors (wariness; Benkada et al., 2020; Kutsukake and Clutton-Brock, 2008; Sommer et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on wariness behavior.

claim: Multiple studies have documented bystander-initiated affiliation with the victim as a means of avoiding redirected aggression or providing substitute reconciliation or consolation.
source: Multiple studies have now documented bystander-initiated affiliation with the victim as a means of avoiding redirected aggression (self-protection) or of providing substitute reconciliation or consolation (Fraser et al., 2009; Fraser et al., 2008; Schino and Marini, 2012; Wittig and Boesch, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on bystander behavior.

claim: There is evidence of bystander-initiated affiliation with the aggressor, which could function as appeasement to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression.
source: There is also some evidence of bystander-initiated affiliation with the aggressor, which could function as appeasement to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression (Cordoni and Palagi, 2015; Palagi et al., 2008; Pallante et al., 2018), and group-wide post-conflict affiliation among bystanders, perhaps to reduce conflict-induced stress (De Marco et al., 2010; Judge and Mullen, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and includes speculation about function.

claim: Research on post-conflict behavior has focussed solely on interactions that occur in the immediate aftermath (usually within 10 min) of an aggressive within-group contest.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, this research has focussed solely on interactions that occur in the immediate aftermath (usually within 10 min) of an aggressive within-group contest; the possibility of delayed post-conflict management behaviour has not been explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: There is increasing experimental evidence that nonhuman animals can remember past events and use information from them when making social decisions later.
source: There is increasing experimental evidence that nonhuman animals can remember past events and use information from them when making social decisions later (Carter and Wilkinson, 2013; Kern and Radford, 2018; Seyfarth and Cheney, 1984; Wittig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Baboons were more likely to offer support in aggressive interactions to individuals they had groomed with earlier (mean: 22 min before; range 10–55 min).
source: For example, baboons (Papio hamadryas ursinus) were more likely to offer support in aggressive interactions to individuals they had groomed with earlier (mean: 22 min before; range 10–55 min), evidenced by a move towards playbacks of grunt calls given during conflicts (Cheney et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Vervet monkeys were more likely to offer coalitionary support to a groupmate in a conflict if they had groomed together within the last hour.
source: Similarly, vervet monkeys (Chlorocebus pygerythrus) were more likely to offer coalitionary support to a groupmate in a conflict if they had groomed together within the last hour (Borgeaud and Bshary, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Chimpanzees that had been involved in an unreconciled conflict earlier in the day (ca 2 hr before) reacted aversively to the playback of an aggressive bark from their former opponent's bond partner.
source: For instance, chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) that had been involved in an unreconciled conflict earlier in the day (ca 2 hr before) reacted aversively to the playback of an aggressive bark from their former opponent's bond partner (a third-party individual likely to offer aggressive support to the former opponent; Wittig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Bystander wasps were more aggressive towards individuals that they had observed to be less aggressive in a previous (10–30 min earlier) fight with a third party.
source: Moreover, it was recently shown that bystander wasps (Polistes fuscatus) were more aggressive towards individuals that they had observed to be less aggressive in a previous (10–30 min earlier) fight with a third party (Tibbetts et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: It is cognitively challenging to use social information gathered in the past, especially where there is reliance on memories of the actions of particular individuals.
source: Investigating the capacity for delayed management behaviour is important because it is thought to be cognitively challenging to use social information gathered in the past, especially where there is reliance on memories of the actions of particular individuals (Frith and Frith, 2012), as other sources of personal and third-party information would likely arise in the interim (Wittig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on cognitive demands.

claim: Numerous species vocalise during or at the end of within-group contests.
source: Numerous species vocalise during or at the end of within-group contests (Bertram et al., 2010; Slocombe et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chimpanzees and rhesus monkeys produce screams when experiencing aggression.
source: For example, chimpanzees and rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) produce screams when experiencing aggression (Gouzoules et al., 1984; Slocombe et al., 2010), whilst little blue penguins (Eudyptula minor) give specific calls after a contest is finished (Waas, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Little blue penguins give specific calls after a contest is finished.
source: For example, chimpanzees and rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) produce screams when experiencing aggression (Gouzoules et al., 1984; Slocombe et al., 2010), whilst little blue penguins (Eudyptula minor) give specific calls after a contest is finished (Waas, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Contest vocalisations likely provide bystanders with valuable information about the occurrence of within-group conflicts as well as about the group members that have potentially been involved and the outcome.
source: These vocalisations likely provide bystanders with valuable information about the occurrence of within-group conflicts as well as about the group members that have potentially been involved and the outcome (Gouzoules et al., 1984; Slocombe and Zuberbühler, 2007; Szipl et al., 2017; Whitehouse and Meunier, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and involves inference about function.

claim: Dwarf mongooses live in cooperatively breeding groups of up to 30 individuals, comprising a dominant breeding pair and non-breeding subordinate helpers of both sexes.
source: Dwarf mongooses live in cooperatively breeding groups of up to 30 individuals, comprising a dominant breeding pair (hereafter 'dominant' individuals) and non-breeding subordinate helpers (hereafter 'subordinate' individuals) of both sexes (Rasa, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on dwarf mongoose social structure.

claim: The most prevalent affiliative behaviour in dwarf mongoose groups is allogrooming.
source: The most prevalent affiliative behaviour in dwarf mongoose groups is allogrooming (hereafter 'grooming'), which underpins the strength of relationships between group members (Kern and Radford, 2021; Kern and Radford, 2016), increases following stressful situations such as intergroup interactions (Morris-Drake et al., 2019), and is traded as a reward for cooperative behaviour (Kern and Radford, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on dwarf mongoose behavior.

claim: Grooming underpins the strength of relationships between group members in dwarf mongooses.
source: The most prevalent affiliative behaviour in dwarf mongoose groups is allogrooming (hereafter 'grooming'), which underpins the strength of relationships between group members (Kern and Radford, 2021; Kern and Radford, 2016), increases following stressful situations such as intergroup interactions (Morris-Drake et al., 2019), and is traded as a reward for cooperative behaviour (Kern and Radford, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Grooming increases following stressful situations such as intergroup interactions in dwarf mongooses.
source: The most prevalent affiliative behaviour in dwarf mongoose groups is allogrooming (hereafter 'grooming'), which underpins the strength of relationships between group members (Kern and Radford, 2021; Kern and Radford, 2016), increases following stressful situations such as intergroup interactions (Morris-Drake et al., 2019), and is traded as a reward for cooperative behaviour (Kern and Radford, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Grooming is traded as a reward for cooperative behaviour in dwarf mongooses.
source: The most prevalent affiliative behaviour in dwarf mongoose groups is allogrooming (hereafter 'grooming'), which underpins the strength of relationships between group members (Kern and Radford, 2021; Kern and Radford, 2016), increases following stressful situations such as intergroup interactions (Morris-Drake et al., 2019), and is traded as a reward for cooperative behaviour (Kern and Radford, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Relatively rare targeted aggression in dwarf mongooses usually acts to reinforce rank and is mainly due to reproductive conflict.
source: Within-group aggressive interactions take two main forms: relatively rare targeted aggression, which usually acts to reinforce rank and is mainly due to reproductive conflict (Rasa, 1977), and relatively common foraging displacements, when a higher-ranking individual displaces a lower-ranking group member from a foraging patch and steals their prey (Sharpe et al., 2016; Sharpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Relatively common foraging displacements occur when a higher-ranking individual displaces a lower-ranking group member from a foraging patch and steals their prey.
source: Within-group aggressive interactions take two main forms: relatively rare targeted aggression, which usually acts to reinforce rank and is mainly due to reproductive conflict (Rasa, 1977), and relatively common foraging displacements, when a higher-ranking individual displaces a lower-ranking group member from a foraging patch and steals their prey (Sharpe et al., 2016; Sharpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Foraging displacements generally involve the higher-ranking individual producing deep growls as it approaches the lower-ranking group member, then hip-slamming the latter away from the food resource, and the displaced individual typically producing high-pitched squeals whilst it retreats.
source: Foraging displacements generally involve the following behavioural sequence: the higher-ranking individual produces deep growls as it approaches the lower-ranking group member; the former then hip-slams the latter away from the food resource; and the displaced individual typically produces high-pitched squeals whilst it retreats (Sharpe et al., 2016; Sharpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing the behavioral sequence.

claim: Natural foraging displacements occur at a mean ± SE observer-detected rate of 2.6 ± 0.2 events per 3-hr observation session, range = 0–10, N = 127 observation sessions across eight groups.
source: To collect data relating to natural foraging displacements (which occur at a mean ± SE observer-detected rate of 2.6 ± 0.2 events per 3-hr observation session, range = 0–10, N = 127 observation sessions across eight groups), we conducted focal watches on foraging subordinates in two situations: immediately after the human observer heard a foraging displacement (conflict situation) and on a matched occasion when there had been no foraging displacement for at least 10 min (control situation).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data collected during the study.

claim: In 2–3 min following both natural foraging displacements, focal foragers spent a significantly greater proportion of time vigilant than in matched-control, non-conflict situations (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 3.154, N = 16, Monte Carlo p<0.001).
source: In 2–3 min following both natural foraging displacements (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 3.154, N = 16, Monte Carlo p<0.001; Figure 2a) and those simulated by playbacks (Z = 3.527, N = 17, p<0.001; Figure 2b), focal foragers spent a significantly greater proportion of time vigilant than in matched-control, non-conflict situations.
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: In 2–3 min following simulated foraging displacements by playbacks, focal foragers spent a significantly greater proportion of time vigilant than in matched-control situations (Z = 3.527, N = 17, p<0.001).
source: In 2–3 min following both natural foraging displacements (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 3.154, N = 16, Monte Carlo p<0.001; Figure 2a) and those simulated by playbacks (Z = 3.527, N = 17, p<0.001; Figure 2b), focal foragers spent a significantly greater proportion of time vigilant than in matched-control, non-conflict situations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: The increased vigilance following foraging displacements indicates that bystanders take notice of conflict between groupmates.
source: The increased vigilance following foraging displacements indicates that bystanders take notice of conflict between groupmates; the experimental results demonstrate that the vocal cues are sufficient to trigger this reaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the vigilance data.

claim: The experimental results demonstrate that the vocal cues are sufficient to trigger increased vigilance reaction.
source: The increased vigilance following foraging displacements indicates that bystanders take notice of conflict between groupmates; the experimental results demonstrate that the vocal cues are sufficient to trigger this reaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the playback experiment results.

claim: The focal individual did not engage in any post-conflict grooming in the 5 min following either natural or simulated foraging displacements.
source: However, the focal individual did not engage in any post-conflict grooming in the 5 min following either natural or simulated foraging displacements; grooming is generally rare (ca 10% of bouts) during foraging periods in dwarf mongooses (Kern and Radford, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational and experimental data.

claim: Grooming is generally rare (ca 10% of bouts) during foraging periods in dwarf mongooses.
source: However, the focal individual did not engage in any post-conflict grooming in the 5 min following either natural or simulated foraging displacements; grooming is generally rare (ca 10% of bouts) during foraging periods in dwarf mongooses (Kern and Radford, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dwarf mongoose bystanders do not appear to engage in post-conflict affiliative behaviour in the immediate aftermath of hearing a within-group contest.
source: Thus, dwarf mongoose bystanders do not appear to engage in post-conflict affiliative behaviour in the immediate aftermath of hearing a within-group contest.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing no grooming in the immediate aftermath.

claim: Six to nine playbacks (mean ± SE: 8.5 ± 0.2, N = 16 trials) were carried out over the course of 3 hr in the afternoon in each trial of Experiment 2.
source: In each trial, six to nine playbacks (mean ± SE: 8.5 ± 0.2, N = 16 trials) were carried out over the course of 3 hr in the afternoon whilst the group were foraging and before they moved towards their evening sleeping refuge (mean ± SE period between the final playback and first grooming bout at the sleeping refuge: 37 ± 5 min, N = 16 trials); individual playbacks were as in Experiment 1 with different tracks played each time.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol and data collection.

claim: The mean ± SE period between the final playback and first grooming bout at the sleeping refuge was 37 ± 5 min, N = 16 trials.
source: In each trial, six to nine playbacks (mean ± SE: 8.5 ± 0.2, N = 16 trials) were carried out over the course of 3 hr in the afternoon whilst the group were foraging and before they moved towards their evening sleeping refuge (mean ± SE period between the final playback and first grooming bout at the sleeping refuge: 37 ± 5 min, N = 16 trials); individual playbacks were as in Experiment 1 with different tracks played each time.
evidence: This describes the temporal delay between playbacks and grooming observations.

claim: 90% of grooming bouts occur at the sleeping refuge (N = 6376 bouts, 174 individuals).
source: If within-group conflict does have delayed effects on affiliative behaviour, we expected an increase in the occurrence of foraging displacements to result in changes in evening grooming levels; 90% of grooming bouts occur at the sleeping refuge (N = 6376 bouts, 174 individuals; Kern and Radford, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature with specific data.

claim: Group members were significantly less likely to be involved in grooming interactions in the evenings following conflict afternoons compared to control afternoons (generalised linear mixed model [GLMM]: χ2 = 5.401, df = 1, p = 0.020).
source: Overall, we found that group members were significantly less likely to be involved in grooming interactions in the evenings following conflict afternoons compared to control afternoons (generalised linear mixed model [GLMM]: χ2 = 5.401, df = 1, p = 0.020; Table 1a; Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Table 1a and Figure 4a.

claim: When considering only those individuals that engaged in grooming, they spent a significantly greater proportion of time doing so on evenings when there had been an earlier simulated increase in conflict compared to control evenings (χ2 = 15.873, df = 1, p<0.001).
source: However, when considering only those individuals that engaged in grooming, they spent a significantly greater proportion of time doing so on evenings when there had been an earlier simulated increase in conflict compared to control evenings (χ2 = 15.873, df = 1, p<0.001; Table 1b; Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Table 1b and Figure 4b.

claim: Individuals that groomed were grooming more frequently on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (χ2 = 8.010, df = 1, p = 0.005).
source: This was because these individuals were grooming more frequently (χ2 = 8.010, df = 1, p = 0.005; Table 1c) and for longer per bout (linear mixed model [LMM]: χ2 = 3.958, df = 1, p = 0.047; Table 1d) after a simulated increase in conflict compared to control conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Table 1c.

claim: Individuals that groomed were grooming for longer per bout on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (linear mixed model [LMM]: χ2 = 3.958, df = 1, p = 0.047).
source: This was because these individuals were grooming more frequently (χ2 = 8.010, df = 1, p = 0.005; Table 1c) and for longer per bout (linear mixed model [LMM]: χ2 = 3.958, df = 1, p = 0.047; Table 1d) after a simulated increase in conflict compared to control conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Table 1d.

claim: Individual identity can be determined from dwarf mongoose close calls.
source: Assuming that aggressors and targets can be identified from their vocalisations—which has been demonstrated for dwarf mongoose close calls (Sharpe et al., 2013), recruitment calls (Kern and Radford, 2016), and surveillance calls (Kern and Radford, 2018)—we predicted that subordinates might engage in either less grooming (due to wariness) or more grooming (as possible appeasement) with aggressors, and that they might engage in more grooming with targets (as possible consolation).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

source: Assuming that aggressors and targets can be identified from their vocalisations—which has been demonstrated for dwarf mongoose close calls (Sharpe et al., 2013), recruitment calls (Kern and Radford, 2016), and surveillance calls (Kern and Radford, 2018)—we predicted that subordinates might engage in either less grooming (due to wariness) or more grooming (as possible appeasement) with aggressors, and that they might engage in more grooming with targets (as possible consolation).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Following conflict trials, subordinates groomed with the dominant pair for a smaller proportion of time than after control trials (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 2.240, N = 8, p = 0.021).
source: We found evidence that simulating aggressive behaviour by a dominant individual during the afternoon resulted in subordinates engaging in less grooming with it at the sleeping refuge that evening. Following conflict trials, subordinates groomed with the dominant pair for a smaller proportion of time than after control trials (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 2.240, N = 8, p = 0.021).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Subordinates engaged in significantly less grooming with the simulated aggressor on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (proportion of time: Z = 2.521, N = 8, p = 0.008).
source: The reduced affiliative engagement by subordinates was driven by a change in behaviour towards the simulated aggressor specifically: subordinates engaged in significantly less grooming with the simulated aggressor on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (proportion of time: Z = 2.521, N = 8, p = 0.008; Figure 5a; proportion of subordinates: Z = 2.201, N = 8, p = 0.033; Figure 5c), but there was no such treatment difference in the grooming of subordinates with the dominant whose calls were not played back (proportion of time: Z = 0.105, N = 8, p = 1; Figure 5b; proportion of subordinates: Z = 0.813, N = 8, p = 0.499; Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: A smaller proportion of subordinates groomed with the simulated aggressor on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (Z = 2.201, N = 8, p = 0.033).
source: The reduced affiliative engagement by subordinates was driven by a change in behaviour towards the simulated aggressor specifically: subordinates engaged in significantly less grooming with the simulated aggressor on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (proportion of time: Z = 2.521, N = 8, p = 0.008; Figure 5a; proportion of subordinates: Z = 2.201, N = 8, p = 0.033; Figure 5c), but there was no such treatment difference in the grooming of subordinates with the dominant whose calls were not played back (proportion of time: Z = 0.105, N = 8, p = 1; Figure 5b; proportion of subordinates: Z = 0.813, N = 8, p = 0.499; Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 5c.

claim: There was no treatment difference in the grooming of subordinates with the dominant whose calls were not played back (proportion of time: Z = 0.105, N = 8, p = 1).
source: The reduced affiliative engagement by subordinates was driven by a change in behaviour towards the simulated aggressor specifically: subordinates engaged in significantly less grooming with the simulated aggressor on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (proportion of time: Z = 2.521, N = 8, p = 0.008; Figure 5a; proportion of subordinates: Z = 2.201, N = 8, p = 0.033; Figure 5c), but there was no such treatment difference in the grooming of subordinates with the dominant whose calls were not played back (proportion of time: Z = 0.105, N = 8, p = 1; Figure 5b; proportion of subordinates: Z = 0.813, N = 8, p = 0.499; Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 5b.

claim: There was no treatment difference in the proportion of subordinates grooming with the dominant whose calls were not played back (Z = 0.813, N = 8, p = 0.499).
source: The reduced affiliative engagement by subordinates was driven by a change in behaviour towards the simulated aggressor specifically: subordinates engaged in significantly less grooming with the simulated aggressor on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (proportion of time: Z = 2.521, N = 8, p = 0.008; Figure 5a; proportion of subordinates: Z = 2.201, N = 8, p = 0.033; Figure 5c), but there was no such treatment difference in the grooming of subordinates with the dominant whose calls were not played back (proportion of time: Z = 0.105, N = 8, p = 1; Figure 5b; proportion of subordinates: Z = 0.813, N = 8, p = 0.499; Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 5d.

claim: Subordinate–subordinate grooming bouts were, on average, significantly longer on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (Z = 2.366, N = 7, p = 0.015).
source: When considering all bouts between subordinate group members, there was no significant treatment difference in the proportion of time spent grooming (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 1.540, N = 8, p = 0.146), but subordinate–subordinate grooming bouts were, on average, significantly longer on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (Z = 2.366, N = 7, p = 0.015; Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: There was no significant treatment difference in the proportion of time spent grooming between subordinate group members (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 1.540, N = 8, p = 0.146).
source: When considering all bouts between subordinate group members, there was no significant treatment difference in the proportion of time spent grooming (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = 1.540, N = 8, p = 0.146), but subordinate–subordinate grooming bouts were, on average, significantly longer on conflict evenings compared to control evenings (Z = 2.366, N = 7, p = 0.015; Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in the average duration of later subordinate–subordinate grooming is in line with the increase in bystander–bystander grooming seen in some species in the immediate aftermath of a contest.
source: The increase in the average duration of later subordinate–subordinate grooming is in line with the increase in bystander–bystander grooming seen in some species in the immediate aftermath of a contest (Judge and Mullen, 2005).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to previous literature.

claim: Bystander-bystander affiliation could reduce the group-wide social anxiety induced by aggression.
source: Such affiliation could reduce the group-wide social anxiety induced by aggression (De Marco et al., 2010; Judge and Bachmann, 2013; Schino and Sciarretta, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about function supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is the first evidence for a change in this direction.
source: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is, to our knowledge, the first evidence for a change in this direction; some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest (Cordoni and Palagi, 2015; Palagi et al., 2008; Pallante et al., 2018), whilst a few others have found no evidence for such an increase (Judge, 1991; Romero et al., 2008; Verbeek and de Waal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison to previous literature.

claim: Some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest.
source: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is, to our knowledge, the first evidence for a change in this direction; some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest (Cordoni and Palagi, 2015; Palagi et al., 2008; Pallante et al., 2018), whilst a few others have found no evidence for such an increase (Judge, 1991; Romero et al., 2008; Verbeek and de Waal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some studies have found no evidence for increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a contest.
source: The later reduction in grooming of aggressors by bystanders is, to our knowledge, the first evidence for a change in this direction; some previous studies have documented increased grooming of aggressors by bystanders in the immediate aftermath of a single contest (Cordoni and Palagi, 2015; Palagi et al., 2008; Pallante et al., 2018), whilst a few others have found no evidence for such an increase (Judge, 1991; Romero et al., 2008; Verbeek and de Waal, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Subordinate bystanders could be avoiding the aggressor to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression.
source: Subordinate bystanders could be avoiding the aggressor to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression, which parallels the main strategy employed in the immediate aftermath of contests by meerkat (Suricata suricatta) and rook (Corvus frugilegus) targets attempting to avoid renewed aggression (Benkada et al., 2020; Kutsukake and Clutton-Brock, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results supported by citations to similar behavior in other species.

claim: Meerkat and rook targets employ avoidance as the main strategy in the immediate aftermath of contests to avoid renewed aggression.
source: Subordinate bystanders could be avoiding the aggressor to reduce the likelihood of redirected aggression, which parallels the main strategy employed in the immediate aftermath of contests by meerkat (Suricata suricatta) and rook (Corvus frugilegus) targets attempting to avoid renewed aggression (Benkada et al., 2020; Kutsukake and Clutton-Brock, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Within-group conflict can affect interactions beyond those between the protagonists.
source: Our results support previous research showing that within-group conflict can affect interactions beyond those between the protagonists and highlight that bystanders can employ different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of the group members involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current results and previous literature.

claim: Bystanders can employ different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of the group members involved.
source: Our results support previous research showing that within-group conflict can affect interactions beyond those between the protagonists and highlight that bystanders can employ different conflict-management strategies depending on the identity of the group members involved.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential responses to simulated aggressors versus non-playback dominants.

claim: Disagreements between two individuals can have wide-reaching and varied implications for affiliative behaviour, which underpins dyadic relationships and social structure in dwarf mongooses and many other group-living species.
source: Disagreements between two individuals can thus have wide-reaching and varied implications for affiliative behaviour, which underpins dyadic relationships and social structure in dwarf mongooses (Kern and Radford, 2021; Kern and Radford, 2018) and many other group-living species (Cameron et al., 2009; Radford and Du Plessis, 2006; Silk et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by the current results and citations to previous literature.

claim: Individuals can retain information relating to earlier within-group conflict and use it when making later decisions about management-related behaviours.
source: The changes in evening grooming patterns once the group had moved from their afternoon foraging areas demonstrate that individuals can retain information relating to earlier within-group conflict and use it when making later decisions about management-related behaviours.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the delayed grooming effects observed in Experiment 2.

claim: The specific reduction in grooming of perceived aggressors and not of non-playback dominants suggests decision-making about which groupmates to groom rather than a general byproduct of an altered physiological state.
source: It is possible that hearing foraging displacements generates stress in bystanders, which could still be elevated on arrival at the sleeping burrow. But the specific reduction in grooming of perceived aggressors and not of non-playback dominants suggests decision-making about which groupmates to groom rather than a general byproduct of an altered physiological state.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential grooming patterns observed.

claim: By using call playbacks, the delayed grooming effects are most likely driven by subordinate bystanders behaving differently towards perceived protagonists, rather than solicitation or rejection of grooming by the latter.
source: Moreover, the use of playback simulations, rather than generation of actual contests, means that the delayed grooming effects are most likely driven by subordinate bystanders behaving differently towards perceived protagonists, rather than solicitation or rejection of grooming by the latter.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism based on the experimental design.

claim: Dwarf mongooses can use vocal information to detect earlier cooperative contributions by groupmates and then reward them later.
source: Previous work has shown that dwarf mongooses can use vocal information to detect earlier cooperative contributions by groupmates and then reward them later (Kern and Radford, 2018); we now provide experimental evidence for delayed post-conflict management behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mongooses and many other social species are constantly monitoring the behaviour and interactions of groupmates, and are using memories of what they learn to inform later decisions.
source: It is thus increasingly apparent that mongooses, as well as many other social species, are constantly monitoring the behaviour and interactions of groupmates, and are using memories of what they learn to inform later decisions (Tibbetts et al., 2020; Wittig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by the current results and citations to previous literature.

claim: The cognitive demands of tracking individuals and their behaviours, remembering that information, and using it when making decisions explain why social interactions within and between groups are believed to be strong drivers of animal intelligence.
source: The cognitive demands of tracking individuals and their behaviours, remembering that information, and using it when making decisions explain why social interactions within (Dunbar and Shultz, 2007) and between (Ashton et al., 2020) groups are believed to be strong drivers of animal intelligence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on the social intelligence hypothesis.

claim: Dwarf mongooses can extract information about within-group conflicts, and the identity of at least some protagonists, from vocal cues alone.
source: Our experiments show that dwarf mongooses can extract information about within-group conflicts, and the identity of at least some protagonists, from vocal cues alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the playback experiments showing differential responses.

claim: Male little blue penguins had an increased heartrate after hearing vocalisations produced by winners of a contest compared to those produced by losers.
source: This adds to a growing body of work demonstrating the ability of social species to garner information acoustically about aggressive interactions (Gouzoules et al., 1984; Slocombe et al., 2010; Slocombe and Zuberbühler, 2007); for example, male little blue penguins had an increased heartrate after hearing vocalisations produced by winners of a contest compared to those produced by losers (Mouterde et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Acoustic monitoring is beneficial as it allows information acquisition in environments where it would be difficult to do so visually or when group members are widely scattered.
source: Acoustic monitoring is beneficial as it allows information acquisition in environments where it would be difficult to do so visually (eg, in low-light and dense vegetation) or when group members are widely scattered and communication is needed over long distances (Bradbury and Vehrencamp, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and general knowledge about acoustic communication.

claim: Acoustic information can be gathered at a relatively low cost: it can be done whilst still actively foraging and at a safe distance that minimises the risk of receiving redirected aggression.
source: Moreover, acoustic information can be gathered at a relatively low cost: it can be done whilst still actively foraging (Hollén et al., 2008) and, in the case of aggressive encounters, at a safe distance that minimises the risk of the information-gatherer receiving any redirected aggression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and logical inference.

claim: Monitoring behaviours acoustically is likely not possible for all within-group interactions or in all social systems.
source: Monitoring behaviours acoustically is likely not possible for all within-group interactions (eg, grooming) or in all social systems, but the calls commonly produced during and at the end of aggressive contests (Bertram et al., 2010; Slocombe et al., 2010) provide a valuable means for bystanders to inform subsequent decision-making.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations and applicability of acoustic monitoring.

claim: All subordinates might be wary of the aggressor and so potentially reduce their grooming with that individual, whereas perhaps only those who are strongly bonded to the target might engage in extra grooming with it.
source: First, all subordinates might be wary of the aggressor and so potentially reduce their grooming with that individual, whereas perhaps only those who are strongly bonded to the target might engage in extra grooming with it (Fraser et al., 2009; Fraser et al., 2008); any such target-related effect might be diluted by considering all subordinates in analyses.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differential strength of responses to aggressors versus targets.

claim: There may be higher selective pressure to discriminate vocalisations from dominant individuals compared to those from other subordinates if the former are more important in terms of social relationships and status.
source: Alternatively, there could be selective attention towards high-ranking individuals (Chance, 1967): there may be higher selective pressure to discriminate vocalisations from dominant individuals cf those from other subordinates if the former are more important in terms of social relationships and status.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to the concept of selective attention.

claim: In many primate species, individuals focus attention on higher-ranking groupmates or those with whom they have an antagonistic relationship, possibly to avoid aggression.
source: In many primate species, for example, individuals focus attention on higher-ranking groupmates or those with whom they have an antagonistic relationship (Keverne et al., 1978; McNelis and Boatright-Horowitz, 1998), possibly to avoid aggression (Schino and Sciarretta, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The study was conducted on Sorabi Rock Lodge, a private game reserve in the Limpopo Province, South Africa.
source: We conducted our study on Sorabi Rock Lodge (24° 11′S, 30° 46′E), a private game reserve in the Limpopo Province, South Africa; full details are available in Kern and Radford, 2013.
evidence: This describes the study location.

claim: At the time of the study (June to October 2019; non-breeding season), eight dwarf mongoose groups (mean ± SE group size: 12.3 ± 1.7, range: 5–16) were fully habituated to the close presence of human observers on foot.
source: At the time of the study (June to October 2019; non-breeding season), eight dwarf mongoose groups (mean ± SE group size: 12.3 ± 1.7, range: 5–16) were fully habituated to the close presence (<5 m) of human observers on foot.
evidence: This describes the study population and timing.

claim: 74.3% of 740 foraging displacement events in 12 groups involved a dominant individual as the aggressor and a subordinate individual as the target.
source: We chose for the playback the combination of a dominant individual as the aggressor and a subordinate individual as a target because this is the most common dyadic pairing observed in natural foraging displacements (74.3% of 740 events in 12 groups).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from the long-term study.

claim: A conflict track concluded with three growls from a dominant aggressor followed by a squeal from a subordinate target.
source: A conflict track concluded with three growls from a dominant aggressor followed by a squeal from a subordinate target, whilst a control track concluded with three close calls from the same dominant individual followed by one close call from the same subordinate individual as in the matched conflict track.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: A control track concluded with three close calls from the same dominant individual followed by one close call from the same subordinate individual as in the matched conflict track.
source: A conflict track concluded with three growls from a dominant aggressor followed by a squeal from a subordinate target, whilst a control track concluded with three close calls from the same dominant individual followed by one close call from the same subordinate individual as in the matched conflict track.
